hints: Notice in the diagram that $V$ is the p.d. across the external variable resistor, while the current $I$ also flows through the internal resistance $r$ inside the dashed box.
Recall the terminal p.d. relation $V = E - Ir$, where $Ir$ is the p.d. lost across the internal resistance.
Check what happens to the term $Ir$ when $I$ increases with $E$ and $r$ fixed, and what this leaves for $V$.
walkthrough: Identify the loop: the e.m.f. $E$ drives current $I$ through the internal resistance $r$ and the external variable resistor in series.
State the governing rule for a real source: terminal p.d. equals e.m.f. minus lost volts, $V = E - Ir$.
Here $E$ and $r$ are fixed properties of the battery, so only $I$ changes when the variable resistor is adjusted.
When $I$ increases, the p.d. across the internal resistance, $Ir$, increases proportionally.
Therefore $V = E - Ir$ must decrease because a larger share of $E$ is dropped across $r$. This is option C.

options.A: The e.m.f. $E$ is a property of the battery and stays constant when only the external variable resistor is adjusted.
options.B: The internal resistance $r$ is a fixed property of the battery and does not increase because $I$ increases.
options.C: A larger $I$ gives a larger lost volts $Ir$ across $r$, so less of the fixed $E$ remains for the terminals and $V = E - Ir$ falls.
options.D: For $I$ to increase the external resistance must decrease, not increase, since $I = E/(r+R)$.
